outcomes: A failed run tells a user what failed, where it failed, and which command can reveal the full structured record
A production-profile run fails closed before execution when readiness diagnostics block it
An agent can retrieve the latest run diagnostics without spending time rerunning the jobs
A measurement consumer can collect a worktree's recorded sessions, in the order they ran, before the worktree is deleted or the store prunes them
A reader of a recorded session can tell which worktree it ran against by comparing one digest, instead of recomputing it against a tree that may have moved
A ledger or benchmark reads what each recorded run cost, over which selection, without writing its own reduction and without counting a nested run as a gate
A reader of a recorded session can tell why a task executed or reused a result from the input digest it was keyed on, without re-running the engine
A runner can identify the actual invocation's recorded plan before its tasks start, without repeating preparation in a separate planning invocation
A reader comparing two recorded sessions of one branch can tell which declared check failed and whether the declarations changed between them
nonGoals: Treating advisory repository hygiene findings as production blockers
Publishing secrets, configuration values, or absolute private paths in diagnostics
Making human terminal text a machine parsing contract
Making a recorded session outlive the worktree it was written in; retention bounds the store, not the worktree

requirements.text: Structured task diagnostics retain severity, code, message, and normalized file, line, and column locations through task and session results.
Human failure output prioritizes located diagnostics, bounds the live presentation, and points to structured output for the complete record.

text: Go and TypeScript test tasks use the same pass, fail and skip summary vocabulary;
causal failure diagnostics obey the CLI report count and message limits with explicit omission accounting, while attributed transcript log events survive batch splitting as session detail.

requirements.text: Doctor is read-only and deterministic; production runs stop before execution on unwaived high or critical findings and fail closed when the gate is unavailable or malformed.
Doctor --machine prints the one-minute load per logical CPU as a ratio, or unknown when the host cannot report it. It takes neither --profile nor --project.

text: Doctor reports a project that has no README.md at its root as an advisory doctor.missing_readme finding, whose remediation names the purpose, commands and documentation a README states.
A template project, which ships README.md.template for the project it renders, and a generated client project are exempt.

requirements.text: Doctor and run diagnostics never reveal configuration values, credentials, or private source contents.

text: An interactive extension subcommand that passes its deadline prints a line naming the command and exits 1, whatever code its process returned.
One whose process ends from a signal exits 1 and prints the signal, except SIGINT, which exits 130 with no line.

requirements.text: Machine JSONL retains a complete sanitized session artifact without changing task or run semantics, and streams one task:start and one task:end per task whatever the run size.

text: The opening scheduler:parallel event carries optional event.sessionId after its v2 plan is written and before tasks start.
Verification and publish-containing runs use the same path and prepare once.
Live and retained streams agree; sessionless schedulers omit the ID.
Readers bind their invocation's event to .putnami/sessions/<sessionId>/plan.json as advisory, untrusted input.
Envelopes, budgets, nested attribution and verdicts are unchanged; missing or elided events provide no early evidence.

Export emits every recorded session still present, oldest first by recorded start time, deduplicated by session id, forwarding the recorded document verbatim so a member a newer producer added survives. --since filters on the recorded start time and is inclusive at the boundary.
Retention is configurable per workspace and its default is unchanged.

`putnami tree fingerprint` prints one digest covering HEAD, the bytes at every tracked path that differs from it (recursing through submodules), and the content of every untracked non-ignored file, from anywhere inside the worktree and without a workspace.
A recorded session carries that same digest, captured before its first task ran, together with the dirty verdict and the head it was taken against.
A producer that cannot determine the tree records no tree block rather than claiming a clean one.
A failed declared check in a recorded session carries a stable diagnostic code; a spec-verification sanction uses features.unresolved_requirement or features.verification_unreadable.
The session carries a digest of the declaration files its declared checks read, taken before its first task and separate from the tree fingerprint: a declaration edit moves it, a code edit does not.
Summary reduces each recorded session to one row: id, start, commands, selection, tasks total/executed/reused, run.cpu.actualMs, wall and outcome, in export's order and with its deduplication.

A run a task spawned names its parent and is marked nested, never counted as a run of its own: --command keeps top-level sessions whose command set is exactly the named list, in any order, and never a nested run whatever it ran.
Structured output carries the rows as an array at every count.
Every task record that reached a verdict carries inputDigest: the cache key it was keyed on, spelled sha256: and 64 lowercase hex, so it moves exactly when the key does.
A skipped record and a task with no cache identity carry none.
Summary --by-digest groups the selected sessions' records by digest in first-recorded order, with records, executed, reused and failed counts and each occurrence's session and reuse;
records without a digest are counted apart.

Doctor reports doctor.agent_hooks_unreachable for a workspace whose explicit install writes extension hooks: per host, a user hook file without a Putnami handler for an event the workspace asks for; a repository no Putnami command recorded; putnami off the PATH.
The finding is advisory and scoped to the workspace root; its remediation names putnami install, a cloud environment's setup script and Codex's /hooks trust step.

Doctor reports doctor.agent_hook_failed when the agent session hook log under the Putnami home holds a failure of this workspace, matched by its workspace root, less than 24 hours old: the finding names the last one, with its time, host, event and error.
The finding is advisory and scoped to the workspace root; an older failure, another workspace's or a log line without a root reports nothing.
putnami install prints, as a warning and before it installs anything, the notice of each retired extension the workspace binds; the install goes on.

Doctor reports doctor.retired_extension_bound for each one, with the notice as its message: the finding is advisory and scoped to the workspace root, and a workspace that binds no retired extension reports nothing.

session.json and the result carry run.orchestration: the wall of each engine phase entered (workspace-load, runtime-sync, probe, selection, plan) and the processes started by kind (job, batch, control, cli, git, other) and git calls by subcommand, from the engine and from jobs built on the extension SDK.
A task record carries its key, lock wait and restore walls. The report fails no run; an unmeasured member is absent, never zero.

Orchestration CPU is the CPU of the engine process, of each extension process without its children, of control processes, of CLI starts made by jobs, and of git started by the engine or an SDK job, which reports its own CPU apart from its children's.
run.orchestration states it, its share of the run's CPU and its ms per selected task; the --trace-profile summary prints the three.
